title: Entering the Mirror Part 2
speaker: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan continue their study of the Platform Sutra and Dogen, following Huineng from the poetry contest into flight. Seiu retells the midnight transmission, Weishun's failure to lift the robe and bowl on Taiyu Ridge, and the question about the original face before parents were born, then recalls a minute of sudden insight on a mountain trail. Kanho stays with Huineng's eight months of pounding rice and the line "simply practice with a straightforward mind," reading it beside "practice and realization are one" in Bendowa and "reality studying reality" in Shoho Jisso. Kanho ends by asking where practice stops and ordinary life begins, with scrubbing the bathroom and folding laundry as examples.

**Seiu Hannah Sullivan:** *An unsurpassed, penetrating and perfect dharma is rarely met with, even in a hundred thousand million kalpas.
Having it to see and listen to, to remember and accept, I vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
I never know whether anyone can hear.
You can hear?
Okay, great.
Well, welcome everyone, once again, and especially to people who haven't been here before, welcome, and to Sunday morning people who are joining us tonight.
That's so great.
Chris and I began study last week of the Platform Sutra and Dogen.
Because they're linked, but everyone might not have heard the first one, I'm going to just do a little summary before we move on.
Chris made three suggestions last week about practice, and I'm going to read them.
I'm going to say them again, because I think they're great, and they're in relation to anything that is said, but also just in general, in your daily life.
First, notice where you abide.
Just notice where the mind takes up residence.
In resentment, in planning, in self-criticism, in fantasy, in fear, in trying to become a better version of yourself.
You don't have to fix it.
Just notice, this is where I'm living right now.
Second, when you notice what might be called the polishing mind, the mind that is urgently trying to improve, repair, or purify itself, pause for a second and ask, "What am I trying to fix right now?
And who is the one who needs fixing?"
Not as a clever Zen question, just a way of slowing down the machinery.
And third, when a difficult feeling comes up, and they do, see if you cannot move in quite so fast to wipe it away.
Not indulging it, not feeding it, not turning it into a story, but also not immediately trying to clean it up.
Let anger be anger.
Let grief be grief.
Let fear be fear.
Let shame be shame.
Without instantly making it "me" or "my failure."
Dust may appear, but maybe you don't have to build a house there.
So I think that forms a bridge between Huineng and Dogen.
Huineng can sound like he's dismissing effort.
Dogen can sound like he's acting for endless effort, but I think they're both trying to free us from the same misunderstanding: the idea that awakening belongs to a perfected self somewhere else.
In fact, even the two poems that Xin Jin and Huineng wrote are not contradictory, and I'll say more about that in a minute.
They might be used as two hands that come together in [unclear: "Ga-Sho"].
Sudden enlightenment and gradual enlightenment are not incompatible.
So let's get back to our story in a little recap.
First, if you're unfamiliar with the tale or you weren't here last time, we're looking at the Platform Sutra, and it's the story of Huineng and his teaching.
He's the sixth ancestor in China, and we mark those ancestors and then move them into Japanese ancestors.
So Dogen is an ancestor in that same line.
So we have this allegedly illiterate young man, Huineng, toiling in the village where he and his mother came to live after his father had been driven out of office and killed.
Lots of changeovers in regimes and lots of violence around it.
After a social fall like that, there's no money for school and one's status is pretty low.
He cuts and sells wood in the market.

One day, he hears a wanderer reciting lines from the Diamond Sutra, which wouldn't be uncommon because most sutras were meant for reciting aloud, since many people were illiterate or didn't have access to printed material.

So the line as translated by Red Pine reads, *one should be non-abiding, thus giving rise to one's mind.* Another translation is *develop a mind which alights on nothing.* It could possibly alight, but it shouldn't stay there.
Awaken the mind without dwelling on anything.
He is galvanized and he resolves to go to the temple of the fifth patriarch, Hongren, asking to become a Buddha.
Hongren accepts him and places him in the pounding room, where the grain is pounded.
Some stories say that he walked a grinding wheel around others, that he pounded, pounded, pounded.
The grain grown at the monastery can become usable food.
This goes on for at least eight months.

When it's announced that Hongren, who's ready to pass on his robes, is holding a poetry contest to discern his successor, Shen Xu, the most revered monk, student, and the obvious choice for a position of Dharma heir, writes this poem on the wall in the monastery.
And he's suggesting that by keeping the mirror of our mind clean and free from dust, polishing that mirror to keep it clean, we will attain enlightenment.
Huineng knew nothing about this until somebody said, "Hey, didn't you know?
Big contest."
And so he asks to be shown into the monastery because he has never been there.
He's just been in that room with the grain.
And he wants to see the wall where the poem [unclear: "Orgata"] was written in order to bow to it.
Meanwhile, Hongren has read that poem.
Hongren's the fifth patriarch.
And he lets Shen Xu know that it's good as far as it goes, but that students reading it or studying with him would not regress.
But it doesn't go far enough.
Write another one.
And yet Shen Xu doesn't.
Maybe he thought he was so good he didn't need to write another one.
So Huineng enters the hall for the first time after being solely in that pounding room, and he takes a look at it and he goes and asks someone to write his poem that he could reveal his mind.
And basically he says, our Buddha nature is forever pure.
Where do you get this dust?
And this is the beginning of what came to be known as the northern and the southern school.
Work, work, work, get your stuff done, get yourself better and maybe then you can become enlightened perhaps.
And from Huineng it's a moment.
It's not that we don't have to work, but we don't have to wait.
So Hongren sees Huineng's poem and he knows that the rice pounder understands what is truly important.
But he doesn't want anyone else to know.
So he says this one doesn't get it either.

But on the third watch, which is essentially midnight, he calls for Huineng, gives him further teaching on the Diamond Sutra, as well as his robe and his bowl, precious objects, saying, Huineng, since ancient times, the lives of those to whom this teaching has been transmitted have hung by a thread.
If you stay here, someone will harm you.
You must leave at once."
This was the beginning of the tradition of the Midnight Transmission Ceremony that everyone who receives the brown robe experiences.
Right, Chris?
So as I said, seventh century China, danger.
We called that first talk the mirror.
This second talk we're calling the flight.
In the dark of night, after receiving transmission, Huineng departs for the Taiyu ridge, and it takes him two months to get there.
He realized that several hundred people had been following him to do him harm.
They were led by a particularly rough character, and he winds up being the only one left.
His name is Weishun.
Huineng places the robe and bowl on a rock and then he hides himself.
But when Weishun tries to take the pieces, he can't lift them.
He can't even move them.
They're so heavy.
He realizes that you can't take the Dharma by force, so he calls out, "I don't want the robe.
I just want the Dharma."
Then Huineng gives him a teaching.
He says, "When you're not thinking of anything good or not thinking of anything bad, what is your original face?
Or what was your original face before your parents were born?"
We've come to know this as a koan, as an iconic question, and one that Dogen used.
What does it mean, we wonder?
Have you ever struggled through trying to intellectually figure out a question like this?
If you have, you know that it's not about braining it out.
Who was I before that? [unclear: "Mostly and"] in the middle of our story, we pause to ask, who am I without my story, my stuff, my identity through my career?
If I don't have my tale to tell, what shines through?
And that goes for others.
Who are you when you strip away your name, social status, achievements, and worries?
It is the you that exists prior to the concepts of good or bad.
It's a prompt to stop logical intellectual thinking.
It invites a sudden flash of light, a flash of insight where the illusion of a separate rigid identity dissolves into what can be known as no self.
I just want to pause here and ask, what is sudden enlightenment?

When I first started thinking about sudden versus gradual enlightenment, I had thought, well, I am definitely the gradual type, because I've never had the experience of sudden enlightenment which persists.
It's like you get your sudden enlightenment and then you're enlightened for the rest of your life.
Well, maybe for some people that is true, but for most of us, the experience of sudden enlightenment occurs in a flash.
One line from the Diamond Sutra is a flash of lightning in a summer storm.
I think we experience occasional flashes of brilliance.
It all makes sense, and that's called satori.
And then it's time to pick up the kids, renew the driver's license, pay the bills, talk with your mother who has dementia who wants to go home from the facility where she lives.
But we have had the experience.
What does it feel like?
How long does it last?
For me, it happened once on a high mountain trail.
A beam of light was shining across a narrow valley, and I realized that I was hearing the voice I'd never heard, seeing the light I thought I would never see.
It was incredibly profound.
It lasted for a minute, and on with my life.
Chris, are you interested in sharing?
Okay, okay, we'll just go on.
So, back to Taiyu Ridge. [unclear: "Additionally, we shun"] the old grizzly pursuer, who's now becoming Huineng's student, says, "Is there any other secret teaching?"
And Huineng says, "What I have taught you is not a secret.
If you reflect on it, you'll find the teaching is within you."
From here, Huineng spends about 18 years in hiding.
He works and lives with a group of hunters, keeping camp when they go out hunting.
This is a time of integration for him, as daily life is his practice.
He's also said to have freed animals from the nets while the hunters are out while he's watching camp, and refusing to eat them when they're cooked for dinner.
He had ample time to prepare for what would be his body of teaching.
Finally, Huineng reaches the temple of Faxing, now known as Guang Shao, where he is recognized as the person who holds the robe and is welcomed to share the dharma.
This happens when he's overhearing two monks arguing over whether the temple flag was moving or the wind was moving.
Huineng intervened and declared, "It is neither the wind nor the flag that is moving.
It is your minds that are moving."
This is where the teaching really takes off.
He calls out, "Good friends."
That's a watchword of the Huineng teaching.
"You already possess the prajna wisdom of enlightenment, but because your minds are [unclear: "diluted"], you need a truly good friend to show you the way to see your nature."
So this works two ways, from without, like a really good teacher, but also from within, since a few verses later, he suggests that the good friend is yourself.
After Huineng comments on the flag issue, or is it the mind issue, he gets on with a core teaching.
*Good friends, this dharma teaching of mine is based on meditation and wisdom.
But don't make the mistake of thinking they are two things.
As long as you think of them as one coming first and giving rise to the other, the dharma will be dualistic.
Simply practice with a straightforward mind.
This is one practice samadhi.*
So let's hear what Chris and Dogen have to say about that.
**Kanho Chris Burkhart:** Testing.
Thank you, Hannah.
We could spend all five weeks on those first 15 paragraphs of the platform sutra, and we wouldn't be done with it.
But it's just so worthwhile to come back to this beginning, because in this opening, Huineng basically shows us, he points us towards the teachings that he will be presenting throughout the sutra.

When I first read the Platform Sutra, all I noticed was the excitement, the mystery of this abbot making the rice pounder, the next Buddha ancestor, the chase and the hiding in the forest and then coming back to the dharma.
It's a really terrific story.
They should make a movie out of it.
This young woodcutter, a poetry contest, the midnight transmission.
And yes, to this day, we receive robe and bowl from our teacher in that ceremony.
The chase over the mountain, we skipped that one.
It's a wonderful story, and it's easy to get carried away by all that drama.
However, staying longer with the Platform Sutra, the more I find myself stopping at quieter teachings that are hidden, but in plain sight.
They just get covered up by the drama and the story.
The sentence that Hannah read earlier, *simply practice with a straightforward mind, this is one practice samadhi*, is one of those core teachings.
I think I may have read right past this sentence for years.
It did sound just too simple, too plain, but now I wonder if Huineng quietly gives us the key to the whole story before the story has even unfolded.
Last week, we talked about entering the mirror, and like Hannah said, this week we are talking about pounding rice.
And I don't think they're two different teachings.
They're the same, viewed from different angles.
Last week, we talked about the possibility that awakening isn't waiting for a perfect version of ourselves, somewhere, sometime in the future.
And this week, Huineng begins to show us what that might look like in practice.
One practice samadhi: walking, standing, sitting, lying down.
We usually wouldn't name these as extraordinary moments.
They are ordinary.
And maybe that is why the Platform Sutra spent so much time in the room where they were pounding the rice.
It's quietly asking us one of the most important questions in Zen.
Where exactly do we imagine our practice is happening?
Because Huineng seems to think the answer is very simple.
Here.
Now.
Wherever we happen to be, whatever we happen to do.
I'd like to carry that understanding with us when we return to the opening pages of the Platform Sutra.
That's one of the beautiful things about Zen.
Most of the time, we just stand around.
And when we get up for kinhin, you may notice that we're not running around the room.
And so sometimes, staying with just a few paragraphs for longer than it might feel comfortable, we begin to realize that they contain far more than what we saw the first five times around.
Today I want to stay with the moment when Huineng arrives at the monastery and spends the next eight months pounding rice, never hearing the teachings.
He didn't even know where the Abbot's room was.
He had to be shown by someone else.
So you may think not much is happening.
But I think both Huineng and Dogen would say exactly this is where it is happening.
And I also admire that young woodcutter who is now just pounding the rice, serving everybody else without receiving what we would expect: teachings, benefits, being supported in his practice.
No, it's not happening.
At least the external things are not happening.
So now I want to touch a little bit more on One Practice Samadhi.
I'm actually going to quote a section from the Platform Sutra.
*One Practice Samadhi means at all times, whether walking, standing, sitting, or lying down, always practicing with a straightforward mind.
The Vimalakirti Sutra says a straightforward mind is the place of enlightenment, and a straightforward mind is the pure land.
Don't practice hypocrisy with your mind while you talk about being straightforward with your mouth.
If you speak about One Practice Samadhi with your mouth, but you don't practice it with a straightforward mind, you're no disciple of the Buddha.
Simply practice with a straightforward mind and don't become attached to any Dharma.*
That is what is meant by One Practice Samadhi.
I'm going to read that key sentence one more time.
*If you speak about One Practice Samadhi with your mouth, but you don't practice with a straightforward mind, you're no disciple of the Buddha.*
I have to admit I love how practical this advice is.
We hear the word samadhi and many of us probably imagine a deep meditative absorption or some extraordinary spiritual state.
Huineng doesn't seem to be very interested in that.
He talks about something much closer to home, a straightforward mind.
What could he mean by that?
I personally don't think that he is talking about being intellectually certain.
I think he is talking about not living a divided life, not saying one thing while secretly living something different, not speaking compassion while in truth nursing resentment.
Has anybody ever done that?
Not talking about non-attachment while clinging to our opinions, not speaking about humility while hoping everybody notices how very, very humble we have become.
*Don't practice hypocrisy with your mind while you talk about being straightforward with your mouth.*
I read this and I don't hear criticism.
I hear an invitation, because I know exactly what he's talking about.
We can say all the right Zen-ish words.

We can quote Dogen, and all the while our mind can be busy defending itself, comparing itself, trying to look competent, replaying old conversations or quietly wishing things were different than they are.
That's a divided mind.
So Huineng is not asking us to become perfect.
He is asking us to become whole.
Dogen picks up the same thread in a way that has always touched me.
In Bendowa, Dogen writes, *practice and realization are one*, such a short sentence.
And yet it changes everything.
If practice and realization are one, then there is no room for pretending.
I can't perform practice today in order to become authentic tomorrow.
I can't wear robes and appear to be practicing while holding resentment and hatred.
Every bow, every period of zazen, every conversation, every apology is already expressing the life I am actually living.
*[Kanho Chris Burkhart and Seiu Hannah Sullivan share this talk.

In some stretches the recording does not show which of them is speaking, so those passages carry no new label.]*
That is the reason why Dogen keeps bringing us back to just sitting.
Sometimes people misunderstand shikantaza as just sitting, meaning merely sitting.
I hear something different.
The just of just sitting means nothing extra, nothing added, nothing taken away, nothing performed.
Just sitting.
Don't do anything but sit.
There is no spiritual costume we put on.
There is just sitting completely as this person in this body at this moment.
In Bendowa, which was Dogen's introduction of Soto Zen to Japan, Dogen has another beautiful phrase for all this.
He calls it chi-juu-yu-zan-mae, the samadhi of receiving and using the Self.
Or the way Norman has translated it in the past, the self-fulfilling samadhi.
I have always enjoyed that expression because it doesn't sound like I need to acquire anything.
There is nothing I can introduce to make this happen.
We can't buy it on Amazon.
We can't buy it on eBay.
But it does sound like inhabiting this life we already have.
There is nothing added and nothing taken away.
When we sit, we're not trying to manufacture a better self.
We are allowing this life to be lived completely.
Nothing added, nothing taken away.
At Samish, I talked about a passage of Shoho Jisso.
Dogen writes, *Reality, studying reality, is called the Buddha ancestor receiving the transmission of Dharma.* Let me repeat that.
*Reality, studying reality, is called the Buddha ancestor receiving the transmission of Dharma.* Well, the first time I read that, it really didn't make a whole lot of sense.
Reality, studying reality?
What does that even mean?
But now I wonder if he was describing exactly what Hoi Nai means by a straightforward mind.
Nothing added, nothing taken away.
A straightforward mind doesn't stand outside reality trying to improve it, because this is what we've got.
It doesn't stand outside of itself trying to become somebody or something else.
Reality is simply [unclear: "needing"] itself.
Sitting is sitting.
Breathing is breathing.
Pounding rice is pounding rice.
The moment doesn't need another version of me to make it complete.
That's why I don't think that one practice, samadhi, is primarily about meditation.
I think it's about honesty, the quiet courage to stop dividing our lives into the person we present and the person we actually are, to stop dividing practice from the rest of our lives.
So now I'm going to change tracks a little.
When Hoi Nai arrives at the monastery, even though the abbot is inviting him to join the monastery, he's not getting invited to the meditation hall.
He's not asked to study sutras.
Nobody is giving him instruction beyond how to pound rice.
So the abbot sends him to work, and that's what he does for the next eight months.
It's amazing that Hoi Nai is not complaining.
He never says, "Hey, I came here to study the Dharma."

I remember when I was at Green Gulch for my second practice period there, my teacher said, "You all have so much excitement in your regular life and you talk so much all the time, so I decided not to teach a class this time."
I was so upset.
I can't afford, due to costs and conditions, to hang out at Tassajara all the time, and I was so looking forward to getting other insights into my teacher's teaching.
So I really deeply admire Hoi Nai.

Listening to all these stories that Hannah recounted and all the stories that we read and hear in Dharma books, it's easy to imagine that awakening happens after something special happens, or in a special place by this really high waterfall or something.
By listening to Dharma talk, not mine but others.
So we pay attention to the dramatic moments because they are dramatic, but the Platform Sutra leaves Hoi Nai pounding away at that rice for eight months.
It lets it become part of the teaching.
Again, I'm going back to Shoho Jisso, the reality of all things.
Dogen writes there, *Reality studying reality is called the Buddha ancestor receiving the transmission of Dharma.* I always keep coming back to that.
Reality studying reality looks like Hoi Nai standing in the rice room pounding rice, lifting a wooden pestle thousands of times.
It looks like silence.
It looks like showing up again tomorrow and doing exactly the same thing.
The practice is not somewhere else.
Reality is not somewhere else and awakening is also not somewhere else.
*Reality, just as it is, is the reality of all things,* says Dogen.
He refuses to let us escape into another world of our imagination.
We want awakening somewhere beyond and outside of this ordinary life.
But Dogen keeps pointing back at this body, this room, this breath, this handful of rice.
I think many of us quietly divide our lives into practice and everything else.
Zazen, chanting, sesshin, that's all practice.
Then we leave the zendo and return to what I've heard some people call real life.
We answer emails, we change the oil in the car, we scrub the bathroom, we care for an aging parent, we fold laundry.
Where exactly do you think practice stops and regular life starts?
I don't think Hoi Nai would understand that question and I don't think Dogen would.
Perhaps that is what Pounding Rice is trying to teach us.
There isn't one place where awakening happens and another place where we scrub the toilet.
There's only one life.
There's only this life.
This is the place where we meet disappointment, where we meet joy, where we discover our impatience and our generosity, grief, love, longing.
Everything is right here in this very moment.
This is the place where I bow.
This is the place where we begin again and again.
That is my Dharma talk for tonight.
But do we have time to go into triads?
We only have five minutes.
You better talk fast.
Triads, did something from tonight.
